LETTER 
Design of Arithmetic Units for Vector Processors Based on Carbon-
Based Technology  
Wei Wu1, 2, 3, Weihua Zhang 1, 2, 3a), Minghui Yin1, 2, 3, Hongwei Liu1, 2, 3, Yunxia You1, 2, 3, Huanhuan Zhou1, 2, 3, Chen 
Wang1, 2, 3, Baisheng Peng1, 2, 3 and Zhiqiang Li1, 2, 3b) 
Abstract Vector processors are widely used in high-performance 
computing (HPC) due to their flexibility and energy efficiency[1-3]. 
However, their performance scaling is increasingly constrained as 
silicon technology approaches its physical limits. This paper 
investigates carbon-based arithmetic units as a promising alternative for 
vector processors. Through simulations, we demonstrate that CNT 
arithmetic unit achieves 33% lower latency than silicon at the 0.5μm 
node. And at sub-10nm technology nodes, CNT-based designs exhibit a 
7× speedup compared to conventional silicon FinFET implementations. 
These results highlight CNT's superior scaling characteristics and its 
strong potential as a next-generation computing technology. 
key words: vector processor, CNFET, semiconductor process, dot-
product, arithmetic logic unit, VLSI design 
Classification: Integrated circuits and VLSI technology  
1. Introduction 
Vector processors[1-3] are gaining increasing popularity 
in high-performance computing due to key advantages: 
data-level 
parallelism 
(DLP) 
[4], 
programmable 
flexibility [5] and energy efficiency[3]. Current vector 
processors mainly employ silicon-based technology. As 
integrated 
circuit 
technology 
advances, 
transistor 
dimensions have been progressively reduced and are 
approaching 
physical 
limits, 
leading 
to 
critical 
challenges: Excessively scaled channel lengths result in 
severe issues such as source-drain tunneling, random 
dopant fluctuations, device mismatch, and self-heating 
effects[6]. These challenges make it difficult for silicon-
based vector processors to achieve further performance 
improvements. 
Carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNFETs) 
have the potential to overcome the limitations of silicon 
MOSFETs[7] due to their exceptional carrier mobility, 
ultrahigh saturation velocity, and long mean free paths[8]. 
With special ballistic conduction mechanisms, CNFETs 
can achieve drive current densities greatly higher than 
those of Si-based devices [9]. Compared to Si-MOSFETs, 
120-nm 
CNFETs 
exhibit 
intrinsic 
gate 
delays 
comparable to 40-nm silicon NMOS devices [10]. 
Digital systems employing CNFETs are projected to 
achieve an order-of-magnitude improvement in energy-
delay product (EDP) relative to Si-CMOS technology 
[11]. Based on the above research, we believe that 
implementing a vector processor with carbon-based 
arithmetic units has the potential to reduce the critical 
path delay and increase the processor's performance. 
This paper explores the application of carbon-based 
technology in arithmetic units for vector processors. We 
extend the HiCoVec processor with a single-cycle 
instruction extension, enabling dot-product operations in 
one cycle. For the physical implementation of the dot 
product unit, a standard cell library was developed based 
on the practical 0.5μm carbon-based process. Building 
upon this, the circuit design, placement, and routing of 
the dot product unit were completed, and its performance 
was simulated and compared with silicon-based circuits. 
To further investigate the potential of carbon-based 
circuits in vector processors, the same dot product unit 
circuit was implemented using a sub-10nm carbon-based 
virtual process and a silicon-based process, followed by 
performance comparisons. Finally, this paper analyzes 
the acceleration mechanism of carbon-based circuits. 
 The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: 
Section 2 reviews existing research on vector processor 
architectures, while Section 3 explores advancements in 
carbon-based semiconductor technologies. Section 4 
formalizes the mathematical definition of the dot-product 
operation. Section 5 details experimental methodologies, 
presenting 
the 
simulated 
dot-product 
unit 
and 
comparative analyses between process-optimized circuit 
variants. Section 6 explains the mechanism of CNFET 
circuits. Finally, Section 7 summarizes the entire text.

2. Vector processor 
Vector processors apply single instructions to multiple 
data elements concurrently[12][13]. Unlike traditional 
SIMD[14] with fixed-width data operations, vector 
architectures employ dynamic vector partitioning for 
parallel processing across vector lanes[2]. This design 
provides greater flexibility than traditional SIMD 
methods. The Vector Register File (VRF) is a key 
component, acting as a cache near the compute unit to 
improve data reuse and reduce memory bandwidth 
pressure[15]. 
Recent advancements in vector processor architecture 
demonstrate 
significant 
progress. 
The 
Zerovex 
system[16] integrates vector and scalar cores within a 
unified architecture, effectively addressing interface 
complexity through three-stage pipeline optimization. 
Empirical studies reveal dual-vector load units enhance 
performance 
metrics, 
with 
memory-constrained 
applications achieving up to 33% acceleration [17]. 
Building upon RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV) 
standards, Spatzformer [4] implements a reconfigurable 
multi-core architecture supporting dynamic mode 
switching between separated and merged configurations, 
effectively 
resolving 
resource 
underutilization 
in 
heterogeneous parallel processing environments. 
3. Carbon-based technology 
CNTs exist as cylindrical carbon allotropes in two 
structural variants: single-walled (SWNTs) and multi-
walled nanotubes (MWNTs). These nanostructures have 
a unique property called chirality, which refers to the 
atomic arrangement of the graphene lattice. Chirality 
determines their electronic, optical, and mechanical 
properties[18]. 
The 
chiral 
configuration 
is 
mathematically expressed by the vector (n, m), where the 
difference (n−m) governs conductivity: multiples of 3 
yield metallic behavior, whereas non-multiples result in 
semiconducting 
characteristics[19]. 
Current 
CNT 
fabrication faces three critical challenges [20, 21] : (1) 
coexistence of metallic and semiconducting types in 
synthesized batches; (2) uncontrollable chiral vector 
variations; and (3) dimensional inaccuracies during mass 
production. 
CNFETs employ carbon nanotubes as charge transport 
channels, with the gate electric field regulating the flow. 
As three-terminal devices comprising source, drain, and 
gate electrodes, CNFETs demonstrate exceptional carrier 
mobility 
with 
ultralow 
static 
power 
dissipation, 
positioning them as promising candidates for next-
generation high-speed low-power integrated circuits [22].

5. Experiment and result analysis 
5.1 HiCoVec 
HiCoVec[24] is a vector processor architecture. This 
configurable SIMD processor (Figure 2 illustrates its 
scalar 
and 
vector 
components) 
comprises 
two 
autonomous 32-bit processing units: a scalar unit and a 
vector unit, which operate independently to enable 
concurrent task execution. The hybrid instruction set 
architecture 
features 
bifurcated 
instruction 
words 
containing distinct scalar and vector fields. This design 
enables simultaneous execution of dual operations within 
a single cycle, while supporting cooperative instruction 
flows that coordinate scalar-vector unit interactions.

We verified the processor's functionality using 
ModelSim simulations (Figure 3). Our architecture

5.2 0.5μm Carbon-based Standard Cell Library 
The implementation of digital circuits relies on standard 
cell libraries, as even the most complex digital circuits 
are built from simple cells within these libraries. All 
standard cells maintain uniform heights with variable 
widths across the library. The power supply, ground lines, 
and input/output port positions within each cell follow 
specific rules, making interconnections between cells 
straightforward and well-organized. This provides 
significant convenience for digital circuit design. 
To implement arithmetic units using carbon-based 
technology, we developed a carbon-based standard cell 
library in 0.5μm technology node, which has 62 cell 
variants across 21 functional categories. The library 
architecture includes combinational logic (INV, NAND, 
NOR, etc.), sequential elements (DFFQ (Figure 5), latch, 
etc.), and P&R auxiliary cells (fillers, tap cells, etc.). For 
these standard cells, we have completed their libraries 
of cell symbols, circuit schematics, layouts, circuit 
performance parameters, functional descriptions, design 
rules, and device model parameters. We have also 
developed standard cell test pattern layouts (Figure 6) for 
fabrication verification and optimized the cell area 
(Figure 7) in compliance with design rule constraints. 
All cells adhere to uniform 24μm height and 15-track 
grid specifications with 3-layer metal stack (M1/M2/M3) 
routing capability, where interconnects follow 0.8μm 
width/spacing design rules compliant with CNFET-
specific parasitic constraints. Using this standard cell 
library enables the synthesis and place-and-route of 
general-purpose digital integrated circuits.

5.3 Dot-product processing unit 
Based on the instruction set expansion requirements of 
HiCoVec, we have designed a dedicated dot-product unit 
to support single cycle operations. The unit is physically 
implemented using our standard cell library. The essence 
of dot-product operation is multiplication and addition. 
For a 4×4bit multiplication operation, it will produce 
four 8bit partial products, which can be implemented 
using an AND gate array. Figure 8 shows the structure, 
with four rows and four columns. The output of the AND 
gate array is the different bits of the four partial products. 
 
 
Fig. 8  AND array structure 
 
To optimize addition speed, the partial products are 
summed through a two-stage Wallace tree structure[25]. 
Each stage reduces three inputs to two outputs. The final 
sum generation requires proper alignment between carry 
signals and corresponding bit positions due to their 
distinct numerical significance, with the interconnection 
methodology visually documented in Figure 9. 
 
 
Fig. 9  Two stages Wallace tree 
 
The conventional approach directly adds four 
operands pairwise, requiring three adder operations. In 
contrast, the Wallace tree method converts adder latency 
into parallel full-adder and half-adder computations, 
requiring only one final adder operation.  
The four 8-bit product terms are compressed into two 
8-bit intermediates using a two-stage Wallace tree. These 
are summed by an 8-bit carry-lookahead adder (CLA), 
with bit 0 generated combinatorially and bit 9 coming 
from the CLA’s carry-out. This allows full 10-bit result 
reconstruction using only an 8-bit adder while preserving 
arithmetic correctness. 
The design methodology is depicted In Figure 10, 
featuring Wallace tree-based multiplier operations and 
partial product summation. Figure 11 displays functional 
verification waveforms, where targeted input excitation 
through single-bit toggling induces expected output 
transitions, validating logical correctness. Figure 12 
shows the dot-product unit layout, implemented with our 
standard cell library, featuring area optimization via 
orthogonal routing and balanced data paths. 
To evaluate architectural advantages, both proposed 
and baseline designs were synthesized using the ASAP7 
[26] Non-Linear Delay Model (NLDM) under TT and 
RVT process corners. The baseline implementation 
employs ripple-carry adders without Wallace tree 
compression or carry-lookahead techniques. Post-
synthesis timing analysis reveals 801.39 ps critical path 
delay for the baseline versus 626.68 ps for the proposed 
architecture, representing a 21.8% latency reduction.

As Table II shows, carbon-based semiconductor 
technology achieves a 7-fold performance enhancement 
over silicon counterparts at equivalent 7 nm technology 
nodes, even with reduced supply voltage. Carbon-based 
circuits improve performance by 62.3% when scaled 
from 7nm to 5nm, while silicon FinFET show less than 
10% improvement under the same scaling [28]. This 
clear contrast originates from carbon-based materials' 
intrinsic advantages—the high carrier mobility, near-
ballistic transport, and low parasitic effects analyzed in 
Section 6. These properties enable both improve 
performance gains and fundamentally greater scaling 
potential than silicon. 
6. CNFET circuit acceleration mechanisms 
Experimental results confirm the superior performance 
of carbon-based circuits over silicon at 0.5μm and sub-
10nm nodes. This section illustrates the fundamental 
reasons through materials and device physics. 
·Carrier Mobility 
CNFETs use carbon nanotubes (CNTs) as channel 
material, offering carrier mobility up to 100× higher than 
silicon[8]. This will increase the conduction current, 
shorten the switching time of AND-array logic gates and 
accelerate partial product generation. 
Additionally, carbon-based devices employ multiple 
CNTs in parallel, further reducing on-resistance and 
increasing current. This avoids the delay accumulation 
caused by insufficient current in silicon-based devices, 
thereby reducing the RC delay in multiplier circuits. 
·Ballistic Transport 
Compared to 500 nm, sub-10 nm scales carbon-based 
performance improves significantly. This is mainly due 
to the high mean free path of carbon-based materials[8], 
enabling ballistic transport at sub-10 nm scales. Carriers 
pass through the channel with almost no scattering, 
greatly reducing the delay in dot-product units. 
·Parasitic Effects 
The diameter of carbon-based channels is extremely 
small, and a gate-all-around (GAA) structure is used to 
enhance gate electrostatic control. This structure reduces 
the overlap region between the channel and the gate 
/source-drain, thereby decreasing parasitic capacitance in 
carbon-based devices and lowering the RC delay of the 
circuit. 
·Interconnects 
Carbon 
nanotube 
interconnects 
exhibit 
superior 
resistance and inductance characteristics compared to 
copper. CNTs have a lower skin effect at high frequency 
[31] and a larger effective conductive cross-sectional 
area, resulting in lower resistance and reduced RC delay. 
 The combined effects of high carrier mobility, ballistic 
transport, reduced parasitic effects, and superior 
interconnects collectively enable carbon-based circuits to 
outperform silicon, especially at sub-10nm scales. 
7. Conclusion 
This study extends the HiCoVec processor with single-
cycle instructions and develops a 0.5μm carbon-based 
standard cell library. Based on this library, we implement 
a carbon-based dot-product unit and explore the 
performance gains achieved by integrating vector 
processor architecture with carbon unit, along with 
analyzing the underlying mechanisms. Using simulation 
models of 0.5μm carbon-based technology, we observe a 
33% reduction in arithmetic unit latency compared to 
equivalent silicon-based simulations. At the 5nm node, 
the carbon-based design achieves 7-fold higher speed 
than silicon FinFET. Below 10nm, carbon-based 
technology 
scales 
more 
efficiently 
than 
silicon, 
maintaining greater performance advantages.

Abstract: Vector processors are widely used in high-performance computing (HPC) due to their flexibility and energy efficiency[1-3]. However, their performance scaling is increasingly constrained as silicon technology approaches its physical limits. This paper investigates carbon-based arithmetic units as a promising alternative for vector processors. Through simulations, we demonstrate that CNT arithmetic unit achieves 33% lower latency than silicon at the 0.5μm node. And at sub-10nm technology nodes, CNT-based designs exhibit a 7× speedup compared to conventional silicon FinFET implementations. These results highlight CNT's superior scaling characteristics and its strong potential as a next-generation computing technology.
